figures.title: The Whole Curriculum Family Tree
figures.subtitle: Every lesson on one chart, grouped the way a label is read.

segments.name: One Chart
segments.text: This is the final review, and it starts with the whole course on one chart. Everything in food falls into three branches, one for each of the first three modules and the same three that the Food Label Tree in Module 5 is built on, and every line on a label belongs to one of them.

segments.name: Macronutrients
segments.text: On the left are the macronutrients, the things you eat in grams: fats, the other lipids like cholesterol, protein, carbohydrates, and water and ethanol. They supply the calories.

segments.name: Micronutrients
segments.text: Next are the micronutrients, eaten in milligrams and micrograms: the fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E and K, the B vitamins and C, and the major and trace minerals.

segments.name: Non-Nutrients
segments.text: The third branch is the non-nutrients, Module 3: things in food, or done to food, that aren't nutrients. Additives, processing and flavorings are what people add or change. Antinutrients and bioactives are plant compounds that simply come with the food. Each box links to its lesson.

segments.name: Where They Show Up
segments.text: Here's the key idea for the rest of this lesson. The first two branches are counted on the Nutrition Facts panel. In the third, additives, processing and flavorings show up in the ingredient list, while antinutrients and bioactives are never printed at all. You find those by knowing the food.

figures.title: Reading a Label Line by Line
figures.subtitle: Which branch each line of the Nutrition Facts panel and ingredient list belongs to.

segments.name: Calories
segments.text: Let's walk down a Nutrition Facts panel. Calories come from the macronutrients: about four per gram of protein and carbohydrate, nine per gram of fat, and seven per gram of alcohol.

segments.name: Fat, Cholesterol, Sodium
segments.text: Total fat, saturated fat and trans fat are the fats lesson. Cholesterol is a sterol, not a fat, so it gets its own line in milligrams. Sodium is a major mineral, and the salt is about two and a half times that number.

segments.name: Carbs, Protein, Micronutrients
segments.text: Total carbohydrate, fiber and sugars are the carbohydrate lesson, protein is protein, and the four required micronutrients are vitamin D, calcium, iron and potassium. On the Daily Value column, five percent or less is low and twenty percent or more is high.

segments.name: The Ingredient List
segments.text: Then the ingredient list. It runs from most to least by weight, and it's where additives, flavor lines and processing words like cultured, enriched or rolled appear.

segments.name: What Is Not Printed
segments.text: Antinutrients and bioactives never get a line. Even a one-ingredient food can carry several of them, as we'll see in the next five foods.

segments.name: The Label
segments.text: Our first food is plain whole-milk yogurt. These are typical values for one cup, for illustration, not any brand's label. The ingredient list is just cultured pasteurized whole milk.

segments.name: Sugars With None Added
segments.text: It shows eleven grams of total sugars but zero added. All of that is lactose, the sugar already in milk, which is why the added sugars line matters.

segments.name: Cultured and Pasteurized
segments.text: Cultured means bacteria turned some lactose into lactic acid. That acid sets the milk protein into a soft gel and gives the tang, which is sour taste from the flavorings lesson. Pasteurized means the milk was heated first to kill harmful microbes.

segments.name: Fat, Protein, Calcium
segments.text: The fat is mostly saturated milk fat, and cholesterol has its own line. The protein is casein and whey, a complete protein rich in leucine. And one cup gives about a quarter of the calcium Daily Value.

segments.name: The Molecules
segments.text: Here are the molecules: lactose, the lactic acid the cultures make from it, leucine from the milk protein, and the calcium ion. Because the cultures use up some lactose, many people who are lactose intolerant manage yogurt better than milk.

figures.title: Canned Beans
figures.subtitle: Salt, an additive, fiber and the antinutrients the can deals with.

segments.name: The Label
segments.text: Next, canned black beans, drained, half a cup. The ingredients are black beans, water, salt and calcium chloride.

segments.name: Salt and an Additive
segments.text: Four hundred milligrams of sodium is about a gram of salt, mostly from the canning liquid. Draining and rinsing washes some away, and no-salt-added cans have far less. Calcium chloride is an additive, E509, a firming agent that keeps the beans from going mushy.

segments.name: Fiber and Protein
segments.text: The fiber is a quarter of the Daily Value in half a cup. The protein is rich in lysine but low in methionine, which is why beans pair so well with grains.

segments.name: What the Can Handles
segments.text: The iron is plant iron, better absorbed with vitamin C in the same meal. And the lines that aren't printed: phytate, which binds some iron and zinc, and lectins, which the canning heat destroys. That's why canned beans are safe straight from the can, while raw or undercooked kidney beans are not.

segments.name: The Molecules
segments.text: In the molecules you can see salt as sodium and chloride ions, lysine with its long side chain, phytic acid with its six phosphate groups that grip mineral ions, and the iron ion it competes for.

figures.title: Rolled Oats
figures.subtitle: One ingredient: starch, beta-glucan fiber and a processing step.

segments.name: One Ingredient
segments.text: Rolled oats have a one-line ingredient list: whole grain rolled oats. Half a cup dry has no sodium, no added sugar, and four grams of fiber.

segments.name: Starch and Fiber
segments.text: Most of the twenty-seven grams of carbohydrate is starch, long chains of alpha-glucose. Part of the fiber is beta-glucan, a soluble fiber made of beta-glucose.

segments.name: Rolled Is a Process
segments.text: Rolled is a processing word. The oats are steamed first, to stop a fat-splitting enzyme that would turn them rancid, then flattened between rollers. The protein is grain protein, low in lysine, so oats pair well with milk, yogurt or beans, and they keep their phytate-rich outer layers.

segments.name: Alpha and Beta
segments.text: Here's the chemistry. Alpha-glucose and beta-glucose differ only in which way one OH group points. Starch is built from alpha-glucose, and your amylase enzymes cut those links into blood glucose.

segments.name: Why It Is Fiber
segments.text: Beta links like this one resist your enzymes, so beta-glucan reaches the gut as soluble fiber and thickens into a gel. About three grams a day from oats, in a diet low in saturated fat, can lower LDL cholesterol, and the FDA allows a heart-health claim for it.

figures.title: Olive Oil
figures.subtitle: Almost pure fat, plus vitamin E and polyphenols.

segments.name: Almost Pure Fat
segments.text: Extra virgin olive oil, one tablespoon. Fourteen grams of fat times nine calories per gram is a hundred and twenty-six, and the label rounds it to a hundred and twenty.

segments.name: Mostly Monounsaturated
segments.text: Ten of those fourteen grams are monounsaturated, mostly oleic acid, the omega-9 fatty acid. And zero cholesterol, because plants don't make it.

segments.name: Extra Virgin
segments.text: Extra virgin is a processing term: the oil is pressed from olives without heat-and-solvent refining, so it keeps its vitamin E and more of its polyphenols, like hydroxytyrosol. Those polyphenols are also why fresh oil tastes peppery and bitter.

segments.name: The Triglyceride
segments.text: Here's a triglyceride, the shape of every fat and oil: glycerol, shaded, holding three fatty acids. The kink at the cis double bond is what keeps olive oil liquid.

segments.name: Vitamin E and Hydroxytyrosol
segments.text: Vitamin E dissolves in the oil and gives up a hydrogen from its OH group to stop fats from going rancid. Hydroxytyrosol has two neighbouring OH groups, and the EU allows a claim that olive oil polyphenols help protect blood lipids from oxidation.

figures.title: Simple Bread
figures.subtitle: Enriched flour, yeast, salt and the crust.

segments.name: Four Ingredients
segments.text: Last, a simple white sandwich bread: enriched wheat flour, water, yeast and salt, and a Contains line for wheat.

segments.name: Enriched Flour
segments.text: Enriched means milling removed the bran and germ, so B vitamins and iron are added back: niacin, thiamin, riboflavin, reduced iron and folic acid. Folic acid has been required in US enriched grain since 1998, to help prevent neural tube defects.

segments.name: Yeast and Crust
segments.text: Yeast ferments sugar into carbon dioxide, which raises the dough, and ethanol, which bakes off. In the oven, browning makes the crust's flavor and a little acrylamide, so toast to golden, not dark brown.

segments.name: Salt and Wheat
segments.text: Bread isn't very salty per slice, but people eat it so often that it's one of the biggest sources of sodium in many diets. And wheat is a major allergen; its gluten proteins form the stretchy network that traps the gas.

segments.name: The Molecules
segments.text: The molecules: folic acid, the stable added form of folate; ethanol and carbon dioxide, the two things yeast makes from each glucose; and acrylamide, which forms from the amino acid asparagine and sugar in dry heat.

figures.title: Putting It All Together
figures.subtitle: The five foods in one table, plus a few things worth knowing.

segments.name: Five Foods
segments.text: Here are all five foods in one table. Notice that even single-ingredient foods touch half the tree, and that each one has something important that isn't on the label at all.

segments.name: Worth Knowing
segments.text: A few last things. Labels round, so zero grams of trans fat can still mean a little. Serving sizes are reference amounts, not advice. Many whole foods have no label, so use a database like USDA FoodData Central. And every number in this lesson is a typical value; always read the package in your hand.
